item.title: Digital divide across territories
item.description:
In short:

  1. The digital divide is not limited to a lack of individual skills: it also covers gaps in equipment and network coverage between territories.
  2. Rural areas and some overseas territories often combine an older stock of equipment with later connection to very high-speed broadband.
  3. Digital usage itself varies by territory, independently of residents’ individual skills.
  4. Local authorities have levers of their own, distinct from skills training, to reduce these territorial gaps.

The digital divide refers to inequalities in access to digital tools and services. At the individual level, it mostly covers a lack of skills, a topic already covered on this blog under digital illiteracy. It also has a territorial dimension: a resident may fully master digital tools and still be penalised by ageing equipment or insufficient network coverage where they live.

item.title: Digital illiteracy: key figures
item.description:
In short:

  1. In France, 15% of the population aged 15 and over is in a situation of digital illiteracy according to Insee, for lack of basic digital skills or internet use.
  2. The phenomenon rises sharply with age: 2% of 15-24 year-olds against 62% of those aged 75 and over.
  3. 29% of French people completed no dematerialised administrative procedure in twelve months, a share that rises to 58% among people with no qualifications.
  4. For a local authority, the response rests as much on the design of online procedures as on the human support that remains necessary.

Digital illiteracy refers to the difficulty or inability to use digital tools independently. Used for several years in public studies, it has become widespread as services, both public and private, have made digital use a condition of access.
